The build stage takes all the source code developers wrote and turns it into a runnable software package - like compiling Java files into a .jar file, or bundling website files into a deployable package.

Think of it like baking a cake - you have all the ingredients (source code files), and "building" mixes and bakes them into one finished cake (a runnable application) that can actually be served.

Example: A Java project's dozens of .java files get compiled and packaged into one single "app.jar" file that can then be run on a server.

What Happens During a Build

• Compiling source code into machine/byte code
• Combining all required libraries (dependencies) the code depends on
• Running quick automated checks (like unit tests) to catch obvious errors early
• Packaging everything into one deployable unit (jar, war, zip, Docker image, etc.)

Example: Maven or Gradle (Java build tools) download required libraries like Spring Boot, compile all code, run unit tests, and produce a single "myapp.jar" file, all with one command.

Build Tools

• Maven / Gradle - for Java projects.
• npm / webpack - for JavaScript/React projects.
• Make / CMake - for C/C++ projects.

Example: Running "mvn package" in a Java project compiles the code, runs tests, and creates the final .jar file automatically - a task that would be very error-prone to do by hand.

Continuous Integration (CI)

Instead of building manually, teams set up an automated system that builds the code every time someone pushes a change - catching build-breaking mistakes almost immediately.

Example: A developer pushes code to GitHub; within a couple of minutes, an automated tool (like GitHub Actions or Jenkins) builds the project and reports whether it succeeded or failed, right in the pull request.

Why This Stage Matters

If the build fails, nothing can move forward - it can't be tested or deployed. Catching build failures early (right when code is pushed) saves the whole team from wasting time debugging a broken build later.

Example: If a developer forgets to add a needed library, the build fails immediately with a clear error, letting them fix it in minutes instead of the problem being discovered days later during deployment.

expert.content:
What Actually Happens at This Stage in a Real Org

The build stage is the entry point of a CI/CD pipeline. Every commit/PR triggers an automated pipeline that compiles code, runs fast tests, performs static analysis, and produces a versioned, immutable artifact ready for deployment. 

Code Push --> CI Server Triggered --> Fetch dependencies
   --> Compile --> Run unit tests --> Static code analysis (SonarQube)
   --> Package artifact (jar/Docker image) --> Push to Artifact Repository
   --> Notify team of pass/fail

Sample CI Pipeline Snippet

# .github/workflows/build.yml
name: Build
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up JDK 17
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          java-version: '17'
      - name: Build with Maven
        run: mvn -B clean package
      - name: Run unit tests
        run: mvn test
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .
Every push automatically triggers this pipeline - if any step fails, the team is alerted immediately and the broken commit never proceeds to later stages.

Key Concepts and Tooling

• Artifact Repository: Nexus, JFrog Artifactory, Docker Hub - stores versioned build outputs so any past version can be redeployed.
• Build reproducibility: the same source code + same dependency versions should always produce the same artifact ("hermetic builds").
• Dependency management: pinning exact library versions to avoid "works on my machine" issues.
• Build caching: reusing previously compiled results to make CI builds much faster.
• Semantic versioning: tagging builds (e.g. 2.3.1) so teams can track exactly what changed.

Common Pitfalls

PitfallImpact
"Works on my machine" builds (no CI, manual local builds)Inconsistent artifacts across environments cause hard-to-diagnose production issues
Unpinned dependency versionsA build that worked yesterday can silently break today when a library auto-updates
Slow, unoptimized build pipelinesDevelopers wait a long time for feedback, slowing down the whole team
Ignoring failed builds ("it'll pass eventually")Broken main branch blocks everyone, and real failures get lost in the noise
Not versioning/tagging build artifactsImpossible to know exactly what code is running in a given environment, or roll back safely

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is Continuous Integration (CI)?The practice of automatically building and testing code every time it's pushed, to catch integration issues early
What is the difference between a build tool and a CI server?A build tool (Maven/Gradle) compiles and packages code; a CI server (Jenkins/GitHub Actions) automatically triggers and orchestrates that build on every change
What is a build artifact?The packaged, deployable output of a build - e.g. a .jar, .war, or Docker image - stored in an artifact repository
Why should builds be reproducible?So the same source and dependencies always produce an identical artifact, avoiding "it worked before" mysteries
What is the purpose of running unit tests during the build stage?To fail fast - catching obviously broken code before it wastes time in later, slower testing stages
What is an artifact repository and why use one?A storage system (Nexus, Artifactory) that keeps versioned build outputs, enabling traceability and easy rollback to any prior version
What does "fail fast" mean in a build pipeline?Ordering pipeline steps so cheap/quick checks (compile, unit test) run before expensive ones, so failures are caught with minimal wasted time

Real-World Architecture Fit

The build stage is the narrow bridge between "source code" and "something that can actually be deployed." Everything upstream (dev) produces source; everything downstream (deployment, monitoring) consumes the versioned artifact this stage produces - nothing later ever touches raw source code again. 

Source (Git) --> CI Server (Jenkins/GitHub Actions/GitLab CI)
   --> Compile + Unit Test + Static Analysis (SonarQube)
   --> Package (jar/Docker image) --> Artifact Repository (Nexus/Artifactory/ECR)
   --> Deployment Stage pulls the EXACT versioned artifact, never rebuilds from source
This "build once, deploy many times" principle is why the artifact repository sits at the center - it guarantees the same tested bits reach staging and production, not two separately-built copies.

Production Problems Caused by This Stage

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
A feature that worked in staging is subtly broken in productionStaging and production were built from source separately instead of deploying the same artifactCompare artifact checksums/versions between staging and prod - they differAdopt "build once, promote everywhere" - build a single immutable artifact and promote it unchanged through environments
A build that passed yesterday fails today with no code changesUnpinned dependency versions - a transitive library silently auto-updatedDiff the dependency lock file / resolved versions between the two build runsPin exact dependency versions and use a lock file (or private mirror) so builds are reproducible
Nobody can tell which exact code version is running in production during an incidentBuild artifacts weren't tagged/versioned, or the CI pipeline didn't stamp the commit SHA into the artifactCheck the artifact repository - artifacts are named "latest" instead of a traceable versionTag every artifact with a semantic version and the source commit SHA, and expose the running version via a health/version endpoint

Anti-Patterns

• Manual, developer-laptop builds pushed to production - no CI at all, "it built on my machine" is the only verification.
• Rebuilding from source for every environment instead of promoting one immutable artifact - risks environment-specific build drift.
• Skipping tests in the build to "make it green faster" - defeats the entire purpose of a build gate.
• Giant, slow build pipelines with no caching - developers wait 30+ minutes for feedback and start ignoring/batching pushes.
• No artifact retention/versioning policy - old artifacts get deleted, making rollback to a known-good version impossible.

beginner.content:
What is the Deployment Stage?

Deployment is the stage where the tested, built software is actually made available to real users - moved from the developer's/tester's environment onto a live server that customers can access.

Think of it like moving into a house after construction and inspection are done - deployment is the "move-in day" for software.

Example: Once a shopping app is fully tested, deployment puts it on the actual company servers so real customers can open the app and start shopping.

Different Environments

Software usually moves through multiple environments before reaching real users:
• Development - where developers build and test locally.
• QA/Staging - a copy of production used for final testing.
• Production - the live environment real users actually use.

Example: A new "dark mode" feature is first deployed to staging so the QA team can verify it, and only after approval is it deployed to production for all users.

Deployment Methods

• Manual Deployment - someone manually copies files/runs commands on the server.
• Automated Deployment - a tool automatically deploys the app with one click or automatically after tests pass (Continuous Deployment).

Example: Instead of a developer manually uploading files via FTP, a pipeline automatically deploys the new version to the server the moment code passes all tests.

Rollback

If something goes wrong after deployment, teams need a way to quickly go back to the previous working version.

Example: After deploying a new payment feature, if customers suddenly can't complete payments, the team quickly rolls back to yesterday's working version while they investigate the issue.

Why This Stage Matters

Deployment is the moment the software actually starts delivering value to real users - all the previous work (requirements, design, coding, testing) only matters once it's safely and reliably deployed.

Example: A perfectly coded and tested feature is useless to the business until it's actually deployed and customers can use it.

expert.content:
What Actually Happens at This Stage in a Real Org

In mature teams, deployment is automated end-to-end through a Continuous Deployment (CD) pipeline. DevOps engineers own the deployment infrastructure, while developers simply trigger (or automatically get) deployments once their code passes all quality gates. 

Build Artifact Ready --> Deploy to Staging --> Automated Smoke Tests
   --> Manual/Automated Approval Gate --> Deploy to Production
   --> Health Checks --> Traffic Gradually Shifted --> Monitoring Confirms Stability

Deployment Strategies

StrategyHow it WorksBenefit
Blue-Green DeploymentTwo identical environments; traffic switches from old (blue) to new (green) instantlyNear-zero downtime, instant rollback
Canary ReleaseNew version rolled out to a small % of users firstLimits blast radius if something breaks
Rolling DeploymentInstances updated gradually, one batch at a timeNo downtime, moderate rollback complexity
Recreate DeploymentOld version stopped completely, new version startedSimple but causes downtime

Sample CD Pipeline Snippet

# deploy stage of a pipeline (pseudo YAML)
deploy_production:
  needs: [build, test]
  when: manual approval granted
  steps:
    - kubectl set image deployment/myapp myapp=myapp:${{ version }}
    - kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp
    - run_smoke_tests.sh
    - if smoke_tests_fail: kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp
Notice the automatic rollback step - if smoke tests fail right after deployment, the pipeline reverts without waiting for a human to notice.

Common Pitfalls

PitfallImpact
Deploying directly to production without staging validationUntested edge cases break the live app for real users
No rollback planA bad deployment causes prolonged outages while the team scrambles to fix forward
Manual, undocumented deployment steps"Bus factor" risk - only one person knows how to deploy, and mistakes are easy under pressure
Deploying during peak traffic hoursAny issue immediately affects the maximum number of users
Configuration drift between staging and production"Works in staging, fails in production" due to environment differences

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?Continuous Delivery means the app is always ready to deploy with a manual approval step; Continuous Deployment auto-deploys every change that passes tests, with no manual gate
What is a blue-green deployment?Running two identical production environments and switching traffic from the old to the new one instantly, enabling near-zero downtime and instant rollback
What is a canary release?Rolling out a new version to a small subset of users/servers first, to catch issues before a full rollout
Why use staging environments before production?To validate the exact build in a production-like setting, catching environment-specific issues before real users are affected
What is a rollback and why is it important?Reverting to the last known-good version quickly when a deployment causes issues, minimizing downtime/impact
What tools are commonly used for deployment automation?Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD, Kubernetes, Ansible, Terraform
What is configuration drift?When environments (staging vs production) gradually diverge in settings/versions, causing inconsistent behavior between them
What is a smoke test after deployment?A quick automated check of critical functionality right after deployment to confirm the new version is healthy before it takes full traffic

Real-World Architecture Fit

Deployment is where a build artifact meets real infrastructure. It sits between the artifact repository and the running production environment, orchestrated by tools that manage traffic shifting, health checks, and rollback - all without a human manually touching a server. 

Artifact Repository --> CD Tool (ArgoCD/Jenkins/GitHub Actions)
   --> Orchestrator (Kubernetes/ECS) pulls image --> Deploy to Staging
   --> Automated smoke tests + approval gate
   --> Deploy to Production (blue-green / canary / rolling)
   --> Load Balancer shifts traffic --> Monitoring Stage watches health
   --> Auto-rollback triggered if error rate/latency SLO breached
Notice deployment hands off directly into monitoring - the health checks that gate a rollout are the same signals the Monitoring stage watches continuously afterward.

Production Problems Caused by This Stage

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
Every deploy causes a visible outage for a few minutesNo blue-green/rolling deployment strategy - a hard "stop old, start new" cutoverCheck the deployment config - it's a "recreate" strategy with no overlap between old and new instancesSwitch to rolling or blue-green deployment so old instances keep serving traffic until new ones are healthy
A bad release stays live for 40 minutes before anyone noticesNo automated health checks or rollback gate after deployment - only manual monitoringReview the pipeline - there's no post-deploy smoke test or automated rollback conditionAdd automated smoke tests and SLO-based auto-rollback immediately after each deployment
"It worked in staging" but fails immediately in productionConfiguration drift - production has different environment variables/secrets/scaling settings than stagingDiff the staging vs production configuration (env vars, resource limits, feature flags)Manage environment config as code (e.g. via a config management tool) so staging and production stay in sync except for intentional differences

Anti-Patterns

• Manual, undocumented deployment steps known only to one person - a single point of failure ("bus factor" risk).
• Deploying straight to production without ever validating in a staging environment first.
• No automated rollback - relying on a human to notice and manually revert during an incident.
• Deploying large batches infrequently instead of small, frequent, low-risk changes - each release becomes high-stakes and stressful.
• Ignoring deployment timing - shipping risky changes right before weekends or peak traffic windows.

beginner.content:
What is the Monitoring Stage?

Once software is live (deployed), monitoring is about continuously watching it to make sure it keeps running correctly, and getting alerted quickly if something goes wrong.

Think of it like a hospital's patient monitor that continuously tracks heartbeat and alerts nurses if something looks abnormal - software monitoring watches the "health" of an application the same way.

Example: For a shopping app, monitoring tracks things like - is the website up? Are pages loading slowly? Are payments failing more than usual?

What Gets Monitored

• Uptime/Availability - is the app up and reachable?
• Performance - how fast are pages loading, how fast do APIs respond?
• Errors - are there crashes, failed requests, exceptions happening?
• Usage - how many users are active, which features are being used?

Example: A dashboard shows that the "checkout" page is taking 5 seconds to load today instead of the usual 1 second - a sign something is wrong that needs investigation.

Alerts

Instead of someone constantly watching dashboards, systems are set up to automatically send a notification (email, SMS, Slack message) when something crosses a dangerous threshold.

Example: If more than 5% of payment requests start failing within 5 minutes, an automatic alert pings the on-call engineer's phone immediately, even at 2 AM.

Logs

Applications continuously write down records of what happened (logs) - which help engineers understand exactly what went wrong when an issue is reported.

Example: When a customer complains "my order didn't go through", engineers search the logs for that customer's order attempt and see the exact error that occurred at that moment.

Why This Stage Matters

Software that seems to "work" during testing can still fail once real, unpredictable users start using it at scale. Monitoring is how a team finds out about problems quickly - often before users even notice or complain.

Example: Monitoring might catch a slow database query causing delays before it gets bad enough that customers start abandoning their shopping carts in frustration.

expert.content:
What Actually Happens at This Stage in a Real Org

Monitoring is a continuous, always-on activity owned jointly by DevOps/SRE (Site Reliability Engineering) teams and the developers who built each service. Modern practice follows "observability" - not just knowing something is broken, but being able to quickly understand WHY. 

Application emits metrics/logs/traces
   --> Collected by monitoring agents (Prometheus, Datadog agent, etc.)
   --> Stored in time-series DB --> Visualized on dashboards (Grafana)
   --> Alert rules evaluated continuously --> On-call engineer paged if breached
   --> Incident triaged using logs/traces --> Root cause fixed

The Three Pillars of Observability

PillarWhat it ShowsCommon Tools
MetricsNumeric time-series data (CPU%, request rate, error rate, latency)Prometheus, Datadog, CloudWatch
LogsDetailed event records for debugging specific incidentsELK Stack (Elasticsearch/Logstash/Kibana), Splunk, Loki
TracesThe full path of a single request across multiple microservicesJaeger, Zipkin, OpenTelemetry

Together these three let engineers answer "is something wrong", "what exactly happened", and "where in the system did it happen" respectively.

Sample Alert Rule (Prometheus-style pseudocode)

alert: HighPaymentFailureRate
expr: (rate(payment_failed_total[5m]) / rate(payment_attempted_total[5m])) > 0.05
for: 5m
labels:
  severity: critical
annotations:
  summary: "Payment failure rate above 5% for 5 minutes"
  action: "Page on-call engineer via PagerDuty"
Key concept: alerts should be based on SLOs (Service Level Objectives) that reflect actual user impact, not arbitrary internal metrics that don't correlate with a real problem.

Common Pitfalls

PitfallImpact
Alert fatigue - too many noisy, low-value alertsOn-call engineers start ignoring alerts, missing the real critical one
Monitoring only infrastructure (CPU/RAM) not business metricsSystem looks "healthy" while checkout conversion actually crashed
No centralized logging across microservicesDebugging an issue means manually SSHing into many servers, wasting critical incident time
No defined SLOs/SLAsTeam doesn't know what "healthy" actually means, so severity of issues is misjudged
Dashboards built but nobody reviews them regularlySlow performance degradation goes unnoticed until it becomes a full outage

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the difference between monitoring and observability?Monitoring tells you something is wrong via predefined metrics/alerts; observability lets you explore unknown issues by correlating metrics, logs, and traces together
What are the three pillars of observability?Metrics (numeric trends), Logs (detailed event records), and Traces (request flow across services)
What is an SLO/SLI/SLA?SLI is a measured indicator (e.g. latency); SLO is the target for that indicator (e.g. 99.9% under 200ms); SLA is the contractual promise to customers tied to SLOs
What is alert fatigue and how is it avoided?Desensitization from too many low-value alerts; avoided by alerting only on user-impacting, actionable conditions tied to SLOs
What is distributed tracing used for?Following a single request as it flows through multiple microservices, to pinpoint exactly where latency or errors are introduced
What is an on-call rotation?A schedule where engineers take turns being reachable to respond to production alerts/incidents outside business hours
Why monitor business metrics, not just infrastructure metrics?Infrastructure can look healthy (low CPU) while a business-critical flow like checkout is silently broken - business metrics catch what infra metrics miss

Real-World Architecture Fit

Monitoring wraps around the live application, continuously feeding signals into dashboards and alerting - closing the loop from "we shipped it" back to "we know it's healthy" and, when it isn't, back into the maintenance stage as a new bug ticket. 

Production App --> emits metrics/logs/traces
   --> Prometheus/Datadog (metrics) + ELK/Loki (logs) + Jaeger (traces)
   --> Grafana dashboards (humans watch trends)
   --> Alertmanager/PagerDuty (machines watch thresholds)
   --> On-call engineer paged --> Incident opened
   --> Root cause found via logs/traces --> Fix flows into Maintenance Stage
This is the feedback loop that makes the SDLC circular rather than a straight line - monitoring is what tells the team a requirement was actually satisfied once real users are involved.

Production Problems Caused by This Stage

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
A major outage runs for hours before anyone at the company notices - customers report it firstNo alerting configured on the metrics that actually reflect user impactCheck alert rules - only infrastructure CPU/memory alerts exist, nothing on error rate or latencyDefine SLOs tied to user-facing behavior (error rate, latency) and alert on those, not just raw infra metrics
On-call engineers start ignoring pages, and a real incident is missedAlert fatigue from too many low-value, noisy alerts over timeReview alert history - dozens of pages per week, most self-resolving within minutesTighten alert thresholds/durations, remove non-actionable alerts, and route only genuinely urgent, user-impacting alerts to paging
Debugging an incident takes 3 hours because engineers manually SSH into a dozen serversNo centralized logging across microservicesCheck whether logs are aggregated in one searchable place or scattered per-instanceShip all logs to a centralized system (ELK/Loki/Splunk) with correlation/request IDs across services

Anti-Patterns

• Dashboards nobody looks at - built once for a demo, never checked again until an incident forces someone to open them.
• Monitoring only "is the server up" instead of business-critical user journeys like checkout or login success rate.
• Alerting on every possible metric instead of only the few that map to real user impact - causing alert fatigue.
• No runbooks - an alert fires but nobody knows what steps to take, wasting critical time during an incident.
• Logging sensitive data (passwords, card numbers) in plaintext - a security/compliance risk baked into the observability setup itself.

beginner.content:
What is the Maintenance Stage?

After software is live, it doesn't just stay untouched forever - the maintenance stage is about ongoing work to keep it running well, fix problems, and make small improvements over time.

Think of it like maintaining a car after buying it - regular servicing, fixing issues, and occasionally upgrading parts to keep it running smoothly for years.

Example: Months after a shopping app launches, the team keeps fixing minor bugs users report and occasionally adds small improvements like a better search filter.

Types of Maintenance

• Corrective Maintenance - fixing bugs that are found after release.
• Adaptive Maintenance - updating software to work with new environments (e.g. a new Android version).
• Perfective Maintenance - improving performance or adding small enhancements based on user feedback.
• Preventive Maintenance - fixing potential problems before they cause issues (e.g. upgrading an old, soon-unsupported library).

Example: Fixing a checkout bug is corrective; updating the app so it works with a new phone's OS update is adaptive; adding a "dark mode" people asked for is perfective.

Handling Bug Reports

Once software is used by many real people, they will find bugs developers didn't catch during testing. Maintenance includes a process for users/support teams to report these issues so they get fixed.

Example: A user emails support saying the app crashes when uploading a large photo - this gets logged as a bug ticket and assigned to a developer to investigate and fix.

Patches and Updates

Fixes and small improvements are released periodically as updates, without needing to rebuild the whole application from scratch.

Example: A mobile app releases "version 2.3.1" which just fixes a login bug, delivered as a small update through the app store rather than a brand-new release.

Why This Stage Matters

Most of a software product's total lifetime and cost is actually spent here, not during initial development - software that isn't maintained becomes outdated, buggy, insecure, and eventually unusable.

Example: An app that never gets security updates becomes an easy target for hackers over time, even if it worked perfectly when it first launched.

expert.content:
What Actually Happens at This Stage in a Real Org

Maintenance is typically the longest phase of a system's life - studies commonly cite 60-80% of total software cost is spent here. In practice, dedicated support/maintenance engineers (or the same product team on a rotation) triage incoming issues, prioritize them, and ship fixes through the normal build-test-deploy pipeline. 

Bug/Feedback Reported --> Triaged & Prioritized (severity/impact)
   --> Assigned to engineer --> Root cause analysis
   --> Fix developed & tested --> Released via normal CI/CD pipeline
   --> Verified in production --> Ticket closed

Maintenance Types (Formal Classification)

TypePurposeExample
CorrectiveFix defects found in productionFixing a null pointer exception crashing checkout
AdaptiveAdjust to environment changesUpdating code for a new OS/library/API version
PerfectiveImprove performance/usabilityOptimizing a slow query, refining UI based on feedback
PreventiveReduce future risk before it becomes an issueRefactoring fragile legacy code, upgrading deprecated dependencies

Managing Technical Debt

A major part of expert-level maintenance is managing technical debt - shortcuts taken earlier (to ship faster) that now slow the team down. Teams typically allocate a fixed percentage of each sprint (e.g. 15-20%) specifically to pay down technical debt alongside bug fixes and feature work, rather than letting it silently accumulate.

Tooling commonly used: Jira/ServiceNow for ticket tracking and SLAs, SonarQube for tracking code quality/ debt trends over time, PagerDuty/Opsgenie for incident-driven maintenance work.

Common Pitfalls

PitfallImpact
No time budgeted for maintenance (100% focus on new features)Bugs pile up, technical debt grows, system becomes fragile over time
No SLA for bug severity levelsCritical production bugs sit unaddressed for as long as minor cosmetic ones
Original developers leave with no documentationNew engineers struggle to safely maintain code they don't understand ("knowledge silo" risk)
Ignoring dependency/security updatesSystem accumulates known vulnerabilities, becoming an easy attack target
Treating every fix as urgentTeam constantly firefights instead of doing planned, sustainable maintenance work

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What are the four types of software maintenance?Corrective (fix bugs), Adaptive (adjust to environment changes), Perfective (improve/enhance), Preventive (reduce future risk)
Why does maintenance typically cost more than initial development over a system's life?Because the maintenance phase spans years, accumulating many small fixes, updates, and enhancements that together exceed the original one-time build cost
What is technical debt?The implied future cost of choosing a quick/easy solution now instead of a better approach that would take longer, which must eventually be "paid back" via refactoring
How should maintenance bugs be prioritized?By severity and business impact (e.g. production outage vs cosmetic UI issue), typically governed by SLA response-time targets
What is a hotfix?An urgent, small, out-of-cycle fix deployed quickly to resolve a critical production issue, bypassing the normal release schedule
Why is documentation important for maintainability?It lets engineers who didn't originally write the code understand and safely modify it, reducing risk when the original author is unavailable
What is preventive maintenance and why do it even without a current bug?Proactively refactoring or upgrading components (e.g. deprecated libraries) before they cause failures, reducing future risk and cost

Real-World Architecture Fit

Maintenance closes the loop back into the exact same pipeline used for original development - a bug found in production doesn't get a special process, it re-enters the normal ticket-to-deploy flow, just triggered by an incident/support ticket instead of a new feature request. 

Monitoring/Support/User Report --> Ticket Created (Jira/ServiceNow)
   --> Triaged by severity/SLA --> Assigned to engineer
   --> Fix goes through: Development --> Build --> Testing --> Deployment
   --> Verified in production via Monitoring
   --> Ticket closed, feeds into technical-debt/velocity metrics
This is why maintenance is often called "the SDLC running in miniature, forever" - every fix is a small trip through the same requirement-to-deployment pipeline the original system went through.

Production Problems Caused by This Stage

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
A security patch breaks an unrelated featureNo regression test suite exists for the legacy code being patchedCheck test coverage on the patched module - little to none, so the side effect went undetectedAdd characterization/regression tests around legacy code before making any change, even "safe" security patches
The same class of bug keeps recurring every few monthsFixes only patch symptoms, root cause analysis is skipped to save timeReview past tickets for that area - multiple "fixes" for what is really one underlying design flawDo proper root cause analysis and fix the underlying issue (e.g. a race condition) rather than repeatedly patching symptoms
A critical production bug sits unfixed for a week while the team ships new featuresNo SLA or prioritization policy separates maintenance work from feature workCheck ticket aging reports - critical bugs and "nice to have" enhancements sit in the same undifferentiated backlogDefine severity-based SLAs and reserve dedicated sprint capacity for maintenance so critical fixes aren't starved by feature pressure

Anti-Patterns

• 100% of every sprint spent on new features, with zero time budgeted for bug fixes or technical debt.
• "If it ain't broke, don't touch it" applied to security-critical dependencies - deferring upgrades until forced by a breach or vendor deadline.
• Fixing bugs without adding a regression test, so the same bug quietly returns later.
• Tribal-knowledge maintenance - only one engineer understands a legacy module, with no documentation to transfer that knowledge.
• Treating every incoming ticket as equally urgent, causing constant context-switching and firefighting instead of planned, prioritized work.

beginner.content:
What is the Retirement Stage?

Retirement (also called "sunset" or "end-of-life") is the final stage where a software system is officially shut down and replaced, because it is outdated, too costly to maintain, or no longer needed.

Think of it like retiring an old car once repairs cost more than it's worth - at some point, the software also reaches a point where it makes more sense to stop using it than to keep fixing it.

Example: A company retires its old billing system once a modern replacement system is ready and all data has been safely moved over.

Why Software Gets Retired

• It has been replaced by a newer, better system.
• It has become too expensive or difficult to maintain (old technology, no one understands the code anymore).
• The business no longer needs that functionality.
• The technology it depends on is no longer supported (e.g. an old programming language/platform).

Example: A company retires an old desktop application once all its customers have moved to the new mobile app version.

Data Migration

Before shutting a system down, any important data it holds usually needs to be moved to the new system or archived safely, so nothing important is lost.

Example: Before retiring an old customer database, the team carefully copies (migrates) all customer records into the new system and double-checks nothing is missing.

Informing Users

Users of the software need advance notice before it's shut down, so they aren't caught off guard and can switch to the replacement in time.

Example: A bank sends emails to customers months in advance saying "Our old mobile app will stop working on March 1st - please download the new app before then."

Why This Stage Matters

A poorly planned retirement can lose important data or leave users stranded without a working system. A well-planned retirement makes sure the transition to whatever comes next is smooth and safe.

Example: If a company shuts down an old system without properly migrating data first, years of important customer records could be permanently lost.

expert.content:
What Actually Happens at This Stage in a Real Org

Retirement (decommissioning) is a formally planned project of its own, usually owned jointly by engineering, product, and compliance/legal teams - especially when regulated data is involved. It is rarely a simple "turn off the server" action. 

Decision to retire (cost/business case)
   --> Stakeholder sign-off --> Data migration/archival plan
   --> User communication & migration window --> Parallel run (old + new side by side)
   --> Cutover to new system --> Decommission infrastructure
   --> Post-retirement data retention per compliance policy

Key Concerns During Decommissioning

• Data retention & compliance - regulations (e.g. financial, healthcare data laws) often require data to be retained for a fixed number of years even after a system is shut down.
• Data migration integrity - verifying every record transferred correctly, with reconciliation reports comparing old vs new system counts.
• Dependency mapping - other internal systems may quietly depend on the system being retired (e.g. via an API or shared database) - these must be found and rerouted first.
• Licensing/infrastructure cost recovery - actually cancelling servers, licenses, and subscriptions tied to the old system to realize the cost savings that justified retirement.

Common Retirement Strategies

StrategyDescription
Big-bang cutoverOld system switched off and new system switched on at one fixed point in time
Parallel runOld and new systems run simultaneously for a period, results compared, before fully switching
Phased/incremental retirementUsers/modules migrated in batches over time rather than all at once
Strangler patternNew system gradually takes over pieces of functionality until the old system has nothing left to do

Common Pitfalls

PitfallImpact
Retiring a system without checking hidden dependenciesOther systems silently break when an undocumented integration suddenly stops working
No data archival planHistorical data needed for audits/legal reasons is permanently lost
Insufficient user notice periodUsers are caught off guard, causing support overload and reputational damage
No rollback plan during cutoverIf the new system has critical issues, there's no safe way back to the old one
Forgetting to actually cancel infrastructure/licensesCompany keeps paying for servers/services nobody uses anymore

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is software retirement/decommissioning?The formal process of shutting down a system that is outdated, replaced, or no longer needed, including data migration and infrastructure cleanup
What is a parallel run during system retirement?Running the old and new systems simultaneously for a period to compare outputs and build confidence before fully cutting over
What is the Strangler Fig pattern?Gradually replacing pieces of a legacy system with a new one until the old system has no responsibilities left and can be safely removed
Why is data retention important even after a system is retired?Legal/regulatory compliance often requires historical data to be kept for a defined period, regardless of whether the originating system is still running
What is dependency mapping before decommissioning a system?Identifying every other system/service that relies on the system being retired, so those integrations can be rerouted safely first
What risk does a "big-bang cutover" carry compared to a phased approach?Higher risk - since everything switches at once, any missed issue affects all users immediately, with less opportunity to catch problems early
Who typically approves a system retirement plan?Business/product stakeholders together with engineering and, for regulated data, legal/compliance teams

Real-World Architecture Fit

Retirement sits at the far end of the pipeline but connects right back to the beginning - it is frequently triggered by (and runs in parallel with) a brand-new requirement stage for the replacement system, with a migration bridge connecting the two. 

Old System (in Maintenance) --+
                              |--> Dependency mapping --> Migration/ETL pipeline
New System (fresh SDLC) ------+          |
                                          v
                              Parallel run --> Reconciliation reports
                                          |
                                          v
                              Cutover --> Old system decommissioned
                                          --> Infra/licenses cancelled
                                          --> Data archived per compliance policy
Notice the retirement of one system and the requirement stage of its replacement typically run side-by-side, connected by a migration/reconciliation pipeline rather than a hard sequential handoff.

Production Problems Caused by This Stage

SymptomRoot CauseDiagnosisFix
An unrelated internal system suddenly starts failing right after an old system is shut downHidden dependency (API call, shared database, batch job) on the retired system was never mappedCheck logs/error traces on the failing system - calls are timing out against an endpoint that no longer existsDo thorough dependency mapping (network traffic analysis, code search) before decommissioning, and reroute all discovered dependencies first
An audit request months later can't be fulfilled because historical records are goneData was deleted at shutdown instead of archived per the required retention policyCheck the decommissioning runbook - no archival step, or retention period was set too shortDefine and follow a compliance-driven data retention/archival plan before any deletion, verified with legal
Customers are locked out and flood support with complaints on cutover dayInsufficient advance notice and no fallback path for users who hadn't migrated yetReview the communication timeline - notices went out days, not months/weeks, before cutoverGive ample advance notice through multiple channels, and offer a grace/fallback period or migration assistance for stragglers

Anti-Patterns

• "Just turn it off" decommissioning - shutting down a system without any dependency mapping or migration plan.
• No reconciliation step after data migration - assuming the migration succeeded without verifying record counts/integrity between old and new systems.
• Retiring infrastructure but forgetting to cancel the underlying licenses/subscriptions, so cost savings never materialize.
• Skipping a parallel-run or phased rollout for a big-bang cutover on a critical system, maximizing blast radius if something is wrong.
• No documented rollback plan if the new replacement system has critical issues discovered right after cutover.

Waterfall - Sequential, phase-gated SDLC model with little rework flexibility

Kanban - Agile-adjacent method visualizing work-in-progress on a board with WIP limits
DevOps - Culture/practice unifying development and operations for faster, safer releases

User Story - Short requirement written from the user perspective: As a... I want... so that...
Acceptance Criteria - Conditions a user story must satisfy to be considered done
Technical Debt - The implied cost of rework caused by choosing a quick/easy solution now

Version Control - System for tracking and managing changes to source code over time
CI/CD - Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment, automating build-test-release
